name: cJSON
workload: Table 10 of the simdjson VLDB 2019 paper parses 14 real-world JSON files (twitter, canada, citm_catalog, mesh, mesh.pretty, apache_builds, github_events, gsoc-2018, instruments, marine_ik, numbers, random, twitterescaped, update-center) in memory, single-threaded, hyperthreading disabled, on an Intel Core i7-6700 (Skylake), reporting parse throughput in GB/s for cJSON, RapidJSON, nlohmann/json and jsmn.
claimed_speedup: cJSON beats nlohmann/json on all 14 files (e.g. gsoc-2018: 0.53 vs 0.14 GB/s; mesh: 0.06 vs 0.05 GB/s) (derived from page data). cJSON beats jsmn on 10 of 14 files. RapidJSON beats cJSON on 13 of 14 files; cJSON is only ahead of RapidJSON on gsoc-2018 (0.53 vs 0.51 GB/s) (derived from page data).
hardware: Intel Core i7-6700 (Skylake), 3.4 GHz, single-threaded, hyperthreading disabled
tradeoffs: cJSON is a simple DOM-only C parser with no SIMD and doubles for all numeric values (precision/int64 caveats); RapidJSON offers a stricter/faster SAX+DOM API and substantially outperforms cJSON on 13 of the 14 files in the same table, so cJSON should not be pitched as beating RapidJSON in general.
caveats: The seed lead's claim that 'the jsmn enricher reported cJSON beats jsmn on 11 of 14 files' does not match a direct read of Table 10, which shows cJSON beating jsmn on 10 of 14 files, not 11 — recorded honestly as 10/14 here. cJSON only wins against RapidJSON on 1 of 14 files (gsoc-2018), so nlohmann/json (won on all 14) is the honest baseline to cite for a 'beats' claim, not RapidJSON. Table 10 numbers are from 2019; cJSON, RapidJSON and nlohmann/json have all been updated many times since, so the gap may have narrowed or widened. nativejson-benchmark (https://github.com/miloyip/nativejson-benchmark) independently lists a cJSON v1.5.0 row with conformance/performance/memory metrics, corroborating that cJSON is a recognized entrant in JSON parser shootouts, but the specific numeric comparison there could not be extracted from the fetched page content, so it is cited only as corroboration, not as the primary evidence.
found_via: seed-record pass: arXiv 1902.08318 (Langdale & Lemire, "Parsing Gigabytes of JSON per Second", VLDB Journal 2019), Table 10; cross-checked https://github.com/miloyip/nativejson-benchmark

name: flatcc
workload: flatbench schema/dataset (same schema and dataset as Google FPL's FlatBuffers benchmark), 1,000,000 iterations of encode and decode/traverse, optimized (-O3 -DNDEBUG) builds, comparing flatcc's generated C reader/builder against Google FlatBuffers' flatc-generated C++ code.
claimed_speedup: Encode: flatcc 626.074 ns/op vs flatc C++ 701.606 ns/op, about 1.12x (~10.8%) faster (derived from page data). Decode/traverse: flatcc 28.652 ns/op vs flatc C++ 28.866 ns/op, effectively tied (~0.7% faster) (derived from page data). Matches the repo's own summary that flatcc is 'a bit faster encoding' while decode is 'close enough... for it not to matter much.'
compiler_and_flags: C++ side: default 'c++' toolchain, -O3 -DNDEBUG -std=c++11; C side: default 'cc' toolchain, -O3 -DNDEBUG -std=c11 (per test/benchmark/benchflatc/run.sh and test/benchmark/benchflatcc/run.sh)
hardware: OS-X, 2.2 GHz Haswell Core i7 (JSON-benchmark section also reports numbers from the same hardware running Ubuntu in VirtualBox)
tradeoffs: flatcc generates C (not C++) code and produces a wire-compatible FlatBuffers binary, so it's usable from pure-C projects; the reported encode gain is attributed by the author mainly to reduced memory allocation rather than a fundamentally different algorithm. Only one schema/dataset is benchmarked, shared with Google's own FlatBuffers benchmark, not a broad corpus.
caveats: Benchmark is first-party (run and published by the flatcc maintainer, not an independent third party) and uses only the default 'c++'/'cc' compiler on the tester's machine rather than a pinned compiler version, though flags (-O3 -DNDEBUG) and CPU model (2.2 GHz Haswell i7) are both stated, which is enough to meet Tier A's 'compiler, flags, and hardware are all stated' bar on flags+hardware even though the compiler vendor/version itself is unpinned. The doc's mention of an OS-X machine and a VirtualBox Ubuntu VM suggests the numbers are several years old and have not been refreshed against current flatc/flatcc releases or hardware.
